facts.claim: Opie and Tatem's A Dictionary of Superstitions (Oxford University Press) gives the earliest dated citation for the rhyme as Charlotte Burne's Shropshire Folk-Lore (1883, page 290), which records it as the saying of 'some Lancashire friends': 'Something old, something new, Something borrowed, and something blue.'
facts.quote: 1883 BURNE Shropshire 290. The dictum of some Lancashire friends … is, 'Something old, something new, Something borrowed, and something blue.'
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09. | CONFLICT: the pillar pack (wedding-traditions fact_14) cites St James's Magazine 1871 via phrases.org.uk; not verified in any scan this run (archive.org 1871 volume search errored). Two Oxford references give 1883 as the first record. [[VERIFY: St James's Magazine 1871 printing against a scan before any 1871 date is stated]]

facts.claim: Simpson and Roud's A Dictionary of English Folklore (Oxford) calls 'Something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue' the widest-known wedding rhyme today and says it was first recorded in Shropshire only in 1883 (Burne, 1883: 290).
facts.quote: The widest-known rhyme today is 'Something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue', first recorded in Shropshire only in 1883 ( Burne , 1883 : 290).
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09.

facts.claim: Burne (1883), as quoted by Opie and Tatem, records that when the wedding gown was white, the 'blue' was carried by making the garters blue.
facts.quote: When the wedding gown is of the orthodox white, the obligation to wear 'blue' is carried out by making the garters of that colour.
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09.

facts.claim: Opie and Tatem quote Folklore (1957, p. 416): the four items were 'almost always worn, even by the most sophisticated brides'.
facts.quote: 1957 Folklore 416. 'Something old, something new, something borrowed and something blue' is almost always worn, even by the most sophisticated brides.

facts.claim: Simpson and Roud say many hold that the borrowed item should be something worn at a previous wedding whose marriage turned out happily, and that the veil is often singled out as the luckiest.
facts.quote: Many say the item borrowed should be something worn at a previous wedding, provided the marriage turned out happily; the veil is often singled out as the luckiest.
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09.

facts.claim: Simpson and Roud say blue is associated with loyalty and true love and hence lucky for brides; the saying 'Marry in blue, Your love will be true' comes from the blue/true rhyme, noticed from the Middle Ages, and Chaucer calls blue a sign of the 'trouthe' (faithfulness) seen in women.
facts.quote: a colour associated with loyalty and true love, and hence lucky for brides, who must wear: Something old, something new, Something borrowed, something blue. In the days when bridal dresses were not necessarily white, blue was a good colour to choose: Marry in blue, Your love will be true. This meaning is derived from the rhyme 'blue/true', which has been noticed from the Middle Ages onwards; Chaucer refers to blue drapery as a 'signe of trouthe that is in wommen sene'
facts.conflicts: Read via Oxford Reference publisher abstract/search excerpt (full entry behind subscription), Apify web-fetch 2026-11-09.

facts.claim: Opie and Tatem's entry 'something blue' records blue being recommended as the lucky colour for a wedding dress, and a 1988 mother of the bride (St Albans) mentioning 'the blue garter of course'.
facts.quote: Her seniors, all … recommended blue as the lucky colour [for her wedding dress]. 1988 [St Albans, Herts.] 'This is my daughter's wedding dress,' she said, and added with a little giggle, 'And the blue garter of course.'

facts.quote: 1946 Mirror 29 Aug. 6 . 'Something old, Something new, Something borrowed, Something blue, And a silver sixpence In your shoe'

facts.claim: Opie and Tatem quote Sean O'Casey's I Knock at the Door (set in Dublin): a bride 'having with her something old and something new, something borrowed and something blue, and a lucky sixpence in her shoe'.
facts.quote: S. O'CASEY I Knock at the Door 103 [Dublin] [On her wedding morning] she was ready for any emergency, so she was, having with her something old and something new, something borrowed and something blue, and a lucky sixpence in her shoe.

facts.quote: A silver sixpence is frequently mentioned: as a gift to a new baby ; as a gift left by fairies for diligent servant girls, or for children shedding a tooth ; as a lucky charm , especially in a bride's shoe

insider_details.detail: Quote the rhyme in the Burne 1883 four-line form and present the sixpence line separately with its 1946 Mirror printing, so every dated version on the page traces to a citation.

For something borrowed, the documented custom is to borrow from a happily married bride, often her veil; an Advisor can suggest asking a married sister, friend or mother early so the piece can be cleaned and fitted.
Something blue has long been worn out of sight (the blue garter), which suits couples who want the tradition without changing the palette.
The sixpence goes in the left shoe; for a destination wedding it is a small coin worth packing in hand luggage with the other heirloom pieces.

often_told: Something old stands for continuity with family; something new for optimism about the future (vendor blogs only; no reference prints these meanings).
Something borrowed 'borrows' happiness from a happily married friend (vendor blogs; Burne 1883 and Simpson and Roud give the happy-bride version, use that instead).
The bride's father places the sixpence in her shoe (Royal Mint blog per pillar pack; page now 404; not re-read).
The rhyme was first recorded in Lancashire in the late 19th century (Royal Mint blog per pillar pack; Burne 1883 does credit 'Lancashire friends', fact_01).
The sixpence line is a later Victorian addition / County Monaghan 1894 (phrases.org.uk and pillar notes; not verified).
Sixpence minting end and loss of legal tender status (Royal Mint Museum page 404; not read; do not state dates).
